panels.figure_caption: This article primarily focuses on the imaging characteristics and differential diagnosis of congenital oral masses, using a prenatally diagnosed Neumann tumor as the central illustrative example. Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 5 and Figure 6 present the same newborn, including prenatal imaging, perinatal planning, postnatal clinical findings, surgical treatment, and histopathological confirmation. Ultrasound examination (USG: GE Healthcare, Chicago, United States) was conducted routinely (A–C) prenatally. Atypical structures were detected during routine ultrasonographic examination at 30 weeks of gestation, raising the suspicion of a congenital mass occupying the oral cavity. Therefore, fetal MRI was performed at 32 weeks and 3 days of gestation for further characterization. In this case, at 34 weeks of gestation, the lesion was described on USG as a tumor filling the oral opening, currently measuring 35 × 28 × 21 mm, with a slightly inhomogeneous structure, and showing clear vascularization. (D) The green area marks the area with increased vascular supply. USG is a very fast, low-cost, and highly effective screening tool for NT and other similar pathologies. At 36 weeks of gestation, another USG concluded that the tumor size had increased and measured 44 × 28 × 27 mm, which prompted a second fetal MRI near-term for more accurate assessment and perinatal planning. In each case of USG, when the result is not clear and the boundaries and adjacent tissue structures close to the lesion are hard to define, an MRI should improve diagnostics. Besides congenital epulis (Neumann tumor), other congenital oral or oropharyngeal lesions that may cause significant airway obstruction at birth include epignathus/oropharyngeal teratoma, extensive lymphatic or vascular malformations, and large cystic lesions of the tongue or floor of the mouth. These conditions may require immediate airway stabilization and, in selected prenatally diagnosed cases, consideration of an EXIT procedure (ex utero intrapartum treatment) [4,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,12].

panels.figure_caption: The Neumann tumor (NT) is a congenital granular cell tumor (CGCT) of the newborn, also known as congenital epulis or soft-tissue oral tumor, found in less than 0.05% of all newborn tumors (NBT) [5,6]. Some studies report that maxillary neonatal epulis is more than three times more common than the mandibular form [4,5,6,7]. CGCT most frequently involves the anterior mucosal alveolar region of the maxilla, whereas the mandible is a less typical site. Lesions are usually solitary, with variable shape and size, while multiple epulides are rare and may cause significant bleeding, ventilation problems, feeding difficulties, or local oral commissure dysfunction. When an oral mass is identified, surgical removal under local or general anesthesia is typically recommended; simple excision with coagulation is usually sufficient, and recurrence or lesion progression was not reported [7,8,9,10]. Ultrasound examination may reveal irregularities at the superficial aspect of the lips and the anterior parts of alveolar ridges, but it is limited in defining deeper soft-tissue relationships, exact lesion extent, and potential airway compromise. In order to improve diagnostic accuracy and assess asymmetry, exophytic lesion size, shape, configuration, and position, as well as tumor relationship to the tongue, palate, jaws, and upper airway, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) should be carefully planned. (A–F) presents fetal MR imaging performed on a 3-Tesla Siemens Magnetom Skyra. The figure shows the fit system (Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) at 32 weeks and 3 days of gestation. The maternal pelvis was examined in three planes using T2-weighted HASTE sequences; the fetal skull in three planes with T2-weighted HASTE and TRUFI, axial DWI and DTI, axial T1 VIBE FS, axial and coronal hemorrhage-sensitive sequences; and the fetal thoracoabdominal region in three planes with T2-weighted TRUFI, coronal DWI-STIR, and coronal and sagittal T1 VIBE FS. Sagittal T2-weighted TRUFI CINE sequences were acquired to assess fetal swallowing. The MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed soft-tissue mass at the level of the oral opening ((A–F); asterisk), located in the midline and slightly off-center, with predominant extraoral protrusion, measuring approximately 15 × 30 × 30 mm. The lesion was inseparable from the lips (A,B) and showed a small intraoral component situated anterior to the tongue (E,F). The tongue appeared normal and showed no continuity with the lesion (B). Beyond partial obliteration of the oral opening, the exophytic mass did not cause significant narrowing within the oral cavity (B) and showed no extension toward the pharynx. A slight S-shaped deviation of the nasal septum was observed, while no cleft palate could be identified. The arches of the maxilla (D) and mandible (E) were intact and could be followed continuously. The pharynx and larynx, as well as the trachea and esophagus, appeared intact. The swallowing mechanism was normal on CINE (motion-capture) sequences. The mass exhibited homogeneous low-signal intensity on T2-weighted images, without evidence of cystic change, fat content, or calcification. Apart from the described lesion, no additional structural abnormalities were identified. Based on its imaging characteristics, the oral soft-tissue lesion was considered most compatible with a granular cell tumor (Neumann tumor). According to serial ultrasound examinations, progressive growth of the lesion raised concern for potential airway obstruction at birth. At 37 weeks and 1 day of gestation, follow-up fetal MRI confirmed a size-progressive soft-tissue mass with the same morphological characteristics and anatomical relationships as observed on the earlier MRI examination. Because ultrasound demonstrated increased vascularization of the lesion, potential connections with facial, labial, or submental arteries and the associated risk of hemorrhagic complications had to be anticipated, while MRI was of limited value in confirming these vascular relationships compared with ultrasound. An EXIT-to-airway procedure was not planned. The prenatal imaging findings relevant to this management included a predominantly extraoral lesion with only a small intraoral component situated anterior to the tongue. There was no significant narrowing within the oral cavity or extension toward the pharynx, and the pharynx, larynx, trachea, and esophagus appeared intact. The tongue was normal, and cine MRI demonstrated preserved fetal swallowing. Taken together, these findings were consistent with a low anticipated risk of critical airway obstruction at delivery and suggested that postnatal airway establishment would likely be feasible without continued placental support. Delivery was therefore scheduled by elective cesarean section at 38 weeks in a tertiary setting, with obstetric, neonatology, pediatric anesthesia, and maxillofacial surgery teams present to permit immediate airway assessment and rescue intervention if required. These imaging findings are in line with previous reports on Neumann tumors and highlight several clinically relevant aspects, particularly regarding airway management and the timing of surgery. NT lesions may extend extra- or intraorally and may cause clinically significant airway compromise [7,8]. This risk is potentially life-threatening and should always be taken into consideration, especially when a life-saving intubation or even tracheotomy of the newborn may be required after delivery. The lesion itself can be surgically removed immediately after birth or within 24–72 h; however, timing largely depends on several factors, including the absence of worrisome bleeding, lack of airway compromise, stable general health of the mother, no restriction in breathing or feeding of the newborn, and the absence of pathological vestibular adhesions of the oral mucosa. Another important aspect when examining the newborn is to assess the extent and diameter of the epulis’ attachment to the oral cavity, as this greatly influences the scope of surgery. Butt et al., along with others [9,10], indicated that the shape and size of these lesions may vary, and some of them may cause airway compromise; rarely, fusion and atresia of nostrils and gums may also be present, which requires immediate surgical intervention. In most cases, a single epulis with well-organized and well-defined borders is found. Before any surgery is scheduled, serious questions should include the following: Is the lesion located to one anatomical area (lips or gingivae)? Does it spread in two or more anatomical areas? Is the bone, skin or muscles involved? Is it placed on vital structures such as the tongue or floor of the mouth? What nerve and vascular proximity is adjacent to the area? And is the scope of any possible vascular components and lesion vascularity known? As shown above, the condition of the lesion base affects decision-making ahead of surgery.

in_text_mentions: A 28-year-old primigravida was referred to the Fetal Medicine Centre due to a suspected fetal facial abnormality at 32 weeks and 4 days of gestation. Prenatal ultrasound confirmed normal fetal growth but revealed a soft tissue mass measuring 27 × 19 mm arising from the upper lip or alveolar ridge (Figure 1A). Fetal swallowing was observed through both the mouth and nose, and tongue mobility was unimpaired.

At 33 weeks and 6 days, a multidisciplinary case conference was held, involving obstetricians, neonatologists, paediatric surgeons, otolaryngologists, and craniofacial surgeons. The origin of the mass remained unclear, with a slight increase in size to 29 × 19 mm (Figures 1B and 2A). Given the potential for airway obstruction at birth, delivery in a tertiary perinatology centre with a team prepared for advanced airway management, including possible intubation, was recommended.
